sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale et complete produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo7/6g.xml (edition Bekker, Open Greek and Latin / First1000Years of Greek, CC BY-SA 4.0), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Le decoupage en 6 chapitres et en sections numerotees suit exactement la structure TEI de la source (chaque section source correspond a un paragraphe de cette traduction) ; les titres de chapitres sont fournis par le traducteur pour la lisibilite, le texte grec n'en comportant pas.

div.head: That the mind follows the body
div.p: That thoughts follow the body, and are not themselves, in their own right, unaffected by the movements of the body, becomes entirely clear in cases of drunkenness and of sickness; for thoughts appear to be greatly altered by the affections of the body.

And conversely, that the body is affected along with the affections of the soul is plain in matters of love, of fear, of grief, and of pleasure. But one might see still more clearly, in things that come about by nature, that body and soul are so joined together as to be, in most cases, the cause of each other's affections.

For no animal has ever come into being of such a kind as to have the outward form of one animal and the mind of another; rather, the body and the soul are always of the same creature, so that a given kind of body must of necessity be followed by a given kind of mind. Moreover, those who are expert in each of the other animals can judge from their outward form — horsemen judging horses, and huntsmen dogs.

If this is true — and it is always true — physiognomy would be possible. Now those physiognomists who came before attempted to practise the art in three ways, each following one of the three. Some practise physiognomy from the genera of animals, positing for each genus a certain form of animal together with a certain mind.

Others, in addition to this, took some particular body, and supposed that whoever had a body like it would also have a soul like it. Others again did the same, but did not draw their evidence from the whole range of animals, but from the human race itself alone, dividing it by nations, according to such differences of appearance and character as there might be — Egyptians, for instance, and Thracians and Scythians — and in like manner made their selection of signs.

Others again drew signs from the characters that show themselves outwardly, observing what disposition follows upon each character — upon the man who is angry, upon the man who is afraid, upon the man given to the pleasures of love, and upon each of the other affections in turn. It is possible to practise physiognomy according to all these methods, and according to others besides, and to make one's selection of signs in dissimilar ways.

Now those who practise physiognomy from characters alone go wrong, first because some who are not the same in nature have the same characters showing on their faces — for instance, the courageous man and the shameless man have the same look, though they are far apart in their dispositions — and second, because at certain times people do not have the same characters, but those of others; for it has happened that men naturally prone to distress have sometimes passed the day pleasantly and taken on the character of the cheerful man, and, conversely, that a cheerful man has grieved, so that the character shown on his face has changed.

Moreover, besides this, one could draw conclusions from but few of these transient appearances. And those who practise physiognomy from beasts do not make their selection of signs correctly either. For it is not possible, having gone through the form of each animal, to say that whoever is similar to it in body will also be similar to it in soul.
For, in the first place, to speak simply, no one would find a man so similar to a beast as that, but only somewhat resembling one in this or that respect.

Moreover, besides this, animals have few signs peculiar to themselves, but many common to several kinds; so that whenever a man resembles one not in what is peculiar to it but in what is common, why should he be thought more similar to a lion than to a deer? For it is reasonable that the peculiar signs should signify something peculiar, and the common signs something common; but the common signs would clarify nothing at all for the physiognomist.

And if one were to select the signs peculiar to each of the beasts, one would not be able to say of what these are signs; for it is reasonable that they should be signs of something peculiar, yet nothing peculiar could be found belonging, in point of mind at least, to any single one of the animals studied by physiognomists: for the lion is not the only courageous creature, but many others are so too, nor is the hare the only cowardly one, but countless others besides.

If, then, neither the selection of common signs nor of peculiar signs yields anything clear, one ought not to examine each of the animals individually, but rather make one's selection from among men who suffer the same affection — for instance, if one is examining the signs of the courageous man, one must take the courageous among animals together as a single class, and inquire what affections belong to all of them alike, yet belong to none of the other animals.

For if one should select in this way, and it should turn out that these are the signs of courage in the animals so chosen, it might be that this is not a mark peculiar to courage among the affections of the mind, but of something else as well; and in that case one would be at a loss to say whether the signs belong to courage or to that other thing. But one must select from the greatest possible number of animals, and animals having no affection of mind in common other than the one whose signs are under examination.

Now those signs that are permanent would signify something permanent; but those that come and go, how could such a sign be true of something in the mind that does not itself remain? For if one should take as a sign something that comes and goes even though it is otherwise permanent, it might indeed be true, yet it would not be a fair sign, since it does not always accompany the thing it is meant to show. And whatever affections arise in the soul without producing any corresponding change in the bodily signs used by the physiognomist could not be reliable indications for the art — just as a physician or a lyre-player cannot be recognized from opinions and branches of knowledge; for one who has learned some piece of learning has changed none of the signs that the physiognomist makes use of.

div.head: The methods and sources of physiognomic signs
div.p: It is necessary, then, to define concerning what matters physiognomy is concerned, since it is not concerned with everything, and from what sources each set of signs is drawn, and then to explain each in turn, taking up in order the more conspicuous cases. Physiognomy, then, is concerned — just as its very name declares — with the natural affections of the mind, and with such acquired ones as, when they supervene, displace the signs studied by physiognomists. What these acquired affections are will be explained later.

I shall now say from what classes the signs are drawn, and they are all these: physiognomists draw their signs from movements, from postures, from colours, from characters as they show upon the face, from the growth of hair, from smoothness of skin, from the voice, from the condition of the flesh, from the parts of the body, and from the general build of the whole body.

Such, in general terms, are the things that physiognomists say concerning the whole classes in which the signs are found. Now if this survey were obscure or not readily intelligible, what has been said would have sufficed.

But as it is, it is perhaps better to go through each point more exactly, concerning everything that is conspicuous among the subjects of physiognomic study, stating what each sign is and to what it refers, so far as this has not been declared in what has already been said. Complexions, then, signify as follows: the ruddy signify a hot temperament and one full of blood; those of a whitish-red signify a good natural disposition, whenever this colour occurs upon smooth skin.

Of hair, the soft signifies cowardice, the coarse, courage. This sign has been drawn from all animals alike; for the most cowardly are the deer, the hare, and sheep, and these have the softest hair, while the most courageous are the lion and the wild boar, and these bear the coarsest hair.

One may observe this same thing also among birds; for, in general, all those that have coarse feathers are courageous, and those that have soft feathers are cowardly, and the same thing may be observed in particular species too, among quails and among cocks.

Likewise, this same thing occurs also among the races of men: those who dwell beneath the Bears (in the north) are courageous and coarse-haired, while those toward the south are cowardly and bear soft hair. Shagginess about the belly signifies talkativeness.

This is referred to the class of birds; for it is peculiar to a bird, among bodily traits, to have shagginess about the belly, and, among mental traits, talkativeness. Flesh that is hard and of good habit by nature signifies dullness of sense, while flesh that is smooth and well-formed signifies a good disposition and instability, unless this occurs upon a body that is strong and has its extremities under control.

Slow movements signify a soft mind, quick movements an ardent one. As for the voice, that which is deep and forceful signifies courage, while that which is high-pitched and slack signifies cowardice. The shapes and the affections that appear upon the face are to be judged by their resemblance to the affection in question.

For whenever a man suffers some affection, he takes on such a look as he has when he is actually undergoing it — for instance, the look of the man who is angry is the sign of the irascible character belonging to the same kind. The male is larger and stronger than the female, and has stronger and more vigorous and altogether better extremities in every point of excellence.

Stronger than the signs drawn from the parts of the body are those drawn from the characters that show themselves outwardly, and those drawn from movements and postures. Generally speaking, to trust a single sign is foolish; but whenever several signs agree in pointing to one and the same thing, one may then more reasonably suppose the signs to be true.

There is also another method by which one might practise physiognomy, though no one has yet attempted it: for instance, if it is necessary that the irascible man, and the man prone to distress, and the man of petty character, should be envious, even though there are no signs of envy itself, it would be possible for the physiognomist, working from those prior signs, to discover the envious man as well; and such a method would belong especially to the man who has practised philosophy.

For to be able to say that, given certain things, a certain other thing must necessarily follow, we should suppose to be peculiar to philosophy — which is sometimes opposed to practising physiognomy directly from the affections and the vices themselves.

Concerning the voice: examining it in respect of affection, one might suppose it to be set down as a sign of spiritedness for two reasons. For the man who is indignant and angry is accustomed to strain his voice and speak sharply, while the man who is in a relaxed state slackens his tone and speaks in a deep voice.

Of animals, again, the courageous are deep-voiced, the cowardly high-voiced: the lion, for instance, and the bull, and the barking dog, and, among cocks, those of stout heart utter a deep cry; whereas the deer and the hare are high-voiced.

But perhaps in these cases too it is better not to make the deepness or the highness of their voice itself the mark of courage or cowardice, but rather to suppose that a voice which is vigorous belongs to the courageous, and one which is slack and feeble to the cowardly.

It is best, whenever the signs do not agree with one another but are opposed, to conclude nothing, unless one knows which, among things thus divided, are the more trustworthy, and, above all, to refer signs to species rather than to whole genera; for these are more akin to the thing sought. For we do not study the physiognomy of the whole human race, but of certain individuals within that race.

div.head: Signs of particular characters
div.p: Signs of the courageous man: coarse hair, an upright bodily posture, bones and ribs and the extremities of the body strong and large, a belly broad and drawn in; shoulder-blades broad and set apart, neither too tightly bound together nor altogether loosened; a neck vigorous, not overly fleshy; a chest fleshy and broad, the hip drawn in, the calves drawn up close beneath; an eye grey-blue, neither too wide open nor altogether closed; the colour of the body somewhat parched; a forehead sharp, straight, not large, lean, neither smooth nor altogether wrinkled.

Signs of the cowardly man: soft, scanty hair, a body held in a crouch, not vigorous; the calves drawn up high; a sallow complexion about the face; weak, blinking eyes, and weak extremities of the body, small legs, thin long hands; a small, weak loin; a strained bearing in his movements; not bold but supine and stupefied in aspect; a facial expression that changes readily, and is downcast.

Signs of the well-endowed man: flesh rather moist and soft, not of good habit nor over-fleshy; the region about the shoulder-blades and neck rather lean, likewise about the face; the shoulder-blades knit together, the lower parts loose; the ribs supple; leaner about the back; the body of a whitish-red and clear colour; the skin fine; hair neither too coarse nor too black; a grey-blue eye, moist.

Signs of the dull man: the region about the neck and legs fleshy and knotted and bound together; a round hip-socket; shoulder-blades drawn up high; a large, round, fleshy forehead; a dull, greenish eye; shins about the ankle thick, fleshy, round; jaws large and fleshy; a fleshy loin; long legs; a thick neck; a fleshy face, rather long. Movements, posture, and facial expression are to be inferred by resemblance.

Signs of the shameless man: a wide-open, bright little eye, eyelids bloodshot and thick; slightly hunched; shoulder-blades raised high; a bearing not upright but rather stooped forward; quick in movement; body inclined to redness; a bloodshot complexion; a round face; a drawn-up chest. Signs of the orderly man —

slow in movement, and slow of speech, a breathy, gentle voice, a lustreless, dark eye, neither too wide open nor altogether closed, slow to blink; for eyes that blink quickly signify sometimes cowardice, sometimes an ardent temper.

Signs of the cheerful man: a forehead of good size, fleshy and smooth, the region about the eyes rather low. The face appears rather drowsy, neither keen-eyed nor pensive. In his movements let him be slow and relaxed; in his bearing and in the expression of his face let him appear, not strained, but good-natured.

Signs of the despondent man: wrinkled faces and lean, downcast eyes — and at the same time, downcast eyes signify two things, one softness and effeminacy, the other dejection and despondency. In bearing he is lowly, and in his movements he seems worn out.

Signs of the effeminate man: a broken-down eye, weak at the knees; an inclination of the head to the right; the carrying of the hands supine and slack, and a double manner of walking, one with the hips swaying, the other with the loins held rigid; and a casting of glances about, such as Dionysius the sophist was said to display.
Signs of the bitter man: a grinning face; a swarthy complexion, lean; the region about the face drawn tight; the face wrinkled and fleshless; straight, black hair.

Signs of the spirited man: an upright body, of good rib-cage in form, cheerful, inclined to redness; shoulder-blades set apart, large and broad; extremities large and firm; smooth about the chest and groin; well-bearded; a full growth of hair, extending downward.

Signs of the gentle man: strong in form, well-fleshed; flesh moist and abundant; of good size and well-proportioned; supine in bearing; the growth of hair drawn back. Signs of the dissembler: a fatty face, and wrinkles about the eyes; the face appears drowsy in expression.

Signs of the mean-spirited man: small-limbed, small and neat, lean, small-eyed and small-faced, such as a Corinthian or a Leucadian might be. Those fond of dice, crook-armed and given to dancing, are fond of abuse — those whose upper lip is raised; and in general those of forward appearance and inclined to redness.

The compassionate are those who are graceful and of a fair complexion, with moist eyes, and whose nostrils are drawn up above, and who are always weeping. These same men are also fond of women and beget more daughters than sons, and are amorous in disposition, and long of memory, and well-endowed by nature, and warm-tempered. The signs of these have been stated. The compassionate man is the wise man, and the coward, and the orderly man; the pitiless man is the ignorant and the shameless.

Good eaters are those in whom the distance from the navel to the chest is greater than that from the chest to the neck. Signs of the lustful man: fair-skinned and shaggy, with straight, thick, black hair; and the temples shaggy with straight hair; a moist, wanton little eye.

Fond of sleep are those who have the upper parts of the body larger, and who are vulture-like and hot-blooded, having flesh of good habit, and are graceful in form, and shaggy about the belly. Those of good memory are those who have the upper parts smaller, and graceful, and rather fleshy.

div.head: The sympathy of body and soul; common and particular animal traits
div.p: It seems to me that soul and body are affected together by one another; and the state of the soul, being altered, alters along with it the form of the body, and again, the form of the body, being altered, alters along with it the state of the soul. For since it belongs to the soul to be distressed and to rejoice, it is evident that those who are distressed are of a gloomier countenance, and those who rejoice are cheerful.

Now if it were the case that, the soul being loosed from grief, the form of the body remained as it was, then body and soul would indeed be affected together in this way, yet would not continue in the same state as one another. But as it is, it is evident that each follows the other. This may become especially clear from the following.

Madness seems to belong to the soul, and physicians, purging the body with drugs and prescribing certain regimens along with these, free the soul from its madness; so that, by these treatments of the body, the form of the body is loosed at the same time as the soul is freed of its madness.

Since, then, both are loosed together, it is clear that they continue together with one another. It is likewise evident that forms come to belong to bodies as resemblances of the powers of the soul, so that all things in animals are indicative of one and the same thing. And many of the things that animals do, some are peculiar affections of each particular kind of animal, and others are common to several.

Now with regard to the works peculiar to the soul, the affections shown in the body are peculiar too, while with regard to the common works, the affections are common. Common, then, are insolence and excess in matters of love. Among crested animals, insolence is common; among asses and pigs, the disposition toward sexual excess.

Peculiar, on the other hand, is scolding among dogs, and painlessness among asses. How one ought to distinguish the common from the peculiar has now been stated. Much practice, however, is needed in all these matters, if one is to become capable of speaking adequately about each of them oneself.

For since things observed upon bodies are said to be referred to resemblances, both those drawn from animals and those drawn from actions, and certain other forms arise also from heat and from cold, and some of these appearances that occur upon bodies use small differences yet are called by the same name — such as pallors that come from fear and those that come from toil (for these are called by the same name, and have but a small difference between them) — and since, the difference being small, it is not easy to recognize it except by having gained a practised eye for the appropriateness of the outward form, the quickest and best method is that which proceeds from this sense of appropriateness, and by using it one may distinguish many things.
And it is useful not only in general, but also for the selection of signs; for each of the things selected must also be fitting, of the kind that the thing selected requires.

Further, in the selection of signs, one must also make use of syllogism, employing it wherever it may be applicable, adding to what is already present what belongs with it — for instance, if a man is shameless and petty, he would also be a thief and illiberal, a thief as a consequence of his shamelessness, and illiberal as a consequence of his pettiness. In each such case, then, one must proceed by fitting the method to the matter in this manner.

div.head: Male and female forms among animals: the lion and the leopard
div.p: Now, first, I shall try to distinguish among animals which of them ought to differ from one another in respect of being courageous or cowardly, just or unjust. One must divide the class of animals into two forms, male and female, attaching to each form what is fitting to it.

They are alike in this: we find, in rearing wild creatures, that the females are gentler and softer in soul than the males, and less given to violent strength, and more receptive of nurture and of being handled by hand. So that, being of this kind, they would presumably be more faint-hearted than the males.

This is plain from our own case too: whenever we are overcome by spiritedness, we become harder to persuade, and we are especially strong in yielding to nothing whatsoever, but are carried toward using force and doing whatever the spirited impulse drives us to.

It seems to me, too, that females are more mischievous than males, and more impulsive and less courageous. Women, and the creatures reared about us, make this quite evident; and as for those that live in the wild, all herdsmen and hunters agree that they are such as has been said.

But this too is plain, that in every kind the female is smaller-headed than the male, and narrower of face, and more slender of neck, and has weaker breasts, and is less broad-ribbed, but is fleshier about the hips and thighs than the male, is knock-kneed, has slender shins, and neater feet, and the whole form of her body inclines more to prettiness than to nobility, and is less sinewy and softer, being made of moister flesh.

The male, in all these respects, is the opposite: its nature is in kind more courageous and more just, while that of the female is more cowardly and more unjust. Things being so, it appears that, of all animals, the lion has partaken most perfectly of the form proper to the male.

For it has a mouth of good size, a face rather square, not overly bony, an upper jaw not projecting but evenly balanced with the lower, a nose rather thick than thin, grey-blue eyes, somewhat hollow, not too round nor too elongated, of moderate size, a brow of good size, a forehead square, somewhat hollow in the middle, and toward the brows and nose there rises from the forehead something like an overhanging cloud.

Above the forehead, along the line of the nose, it has hair inclining outward, as it were bristling; a head of moderate size, a neck of good length, of proportionate thickness, covered with tawny hair, neither shaggy nor too smooth-lying; the region about the collarbones looser rather than closely bound; robust shoulders, and a youthful chest, and the region between the shoulder-blades broad and well-ribbed and fittingly formed at the back; the creature is leaner about the hips and thighs; legs vigorous and sinewy, a youthful gait, and the whole body jointed and sinewy, neither too hard nor too moist.

It walks slowly, taking great strides, and swaying at the shoulders as it goes. Such, then, is its bodily form; as for its soul, it is generous and free, magnanimous and fond of victory, and gentle and just and affectionate toward whatever it associates with.
The leopard, of those creatures reputed courageous, is more of a female form, except as to its legs; and in these it has a certain vigour that produces some effect of strength.

For it has a small face, a large mouth, small, whitish, hollow eyes, but rather prominent; a rather elongated forehead, more rounded than flat toward the ears; a neck excessively long and thin, a narrow-ribbed chest, a long back, fleshy hips and thighs, but flatter about the flanks and belly; its colour is variegated, and its whole form is disjointed and disproportionate.

Such, then, is the form of its body; as for its soul, it is petty, thievish, and, to put it simply, deceitful. The most conspicuous of the animals reputed courageous, then, that have partaken of the male form and of the female form respectively, have now been described. The rest are easy enough to consider, once one has these as a model. Whatever, among animals, is fitting to observe for the purposes of physiognomy will be stated in the section on the selection of signs.

div.head: A catalogue of bodily signs and the characters they indicate
div.p: The selection of signs, as it applies to men, is made as follows. Whoever has feet well-formed and large, well-jointed and sinewy, is vigorous in soul; this is referred to the male sex. Whoever has feet small, narrow, ill-jointed, and pleasanter to look at than strong, is soft in soul; this is referred to the female sex.

Those whose toes are crooked are shameless; this is referred to the birds of crooked talon. Those whose toes are pressed close together are fearful; this is referred to the narrow-footed marsh-birds, the quails.
Those whose ankles are sinewy and well-jointed are stout of soul; this is referred to the male sex. Those whose ankles are fleshy and ill-jointed are soft of soul; this is referred to the female sex.

Those who have shins well-jointed, sinewy, and vigorous are stout of soul; this is referred to the male. Those who have shins thin and sinewy are lustful; this is referred to birds. Those who have shins excessively fleshy, as though on the point of bursting, are disgusting and shameless; this is referred to their general appropriateness.

Those knock-kneed are effeminate; this is referred to appropriateness. Those who have thighs bony and sinewy are vigorous; this is referred to the male. Those who have thighs bony but overly fleshy are soft; this is referred to the female.

Those who have the buttocks lean and bony are vigorous; those who have them fleshy and fat are soft; those who have but little flesh there, as it were shrunken away, are of bad character; this is referred to monkeys.

Those who are girdled tight are fond of hunting; this is referred to lions and dogs; one might observe, indeed, that the keenest hunting-dogs are tightly girdled. Those whose belly-region is lank are vigorous; this is referred to the male.

Those who are not lank there are soft; this is referred to appropriateness. Those whose back is of good size and vigorous are stout of soul; this is referred to the male. Those who have a narrow, weak back are soft; this is referred to the female.

Those broad in the ribs are stout of soul; this is referred to the male. Those narrow in the ribs are soft of soul; this is referred to the female. Those who are puffed out about the ribs, as though inflated, are chattering and foolish talkers; this is referred to oxen or to frogs.

Those in whom the distance from the navel to the top of the chest is greater than that from the top of the chest to the neck are gluttonous and dull; gluttonous, because they have a large vessel to receive their food, and dull, because the region of the senses is more cramped, being joined closely to the food-receiving part, so that the senses are weighed down by the fullness or emptiness of the food.
Those who have a large, well-jointed chest are stout of soul; this is referred to the male.

Those who have the region between the shoulder-blades large, well-fleshed, and well-jointed are stout of soul; this is referred to the male. Those who have it weak, fleshless, and ill-jointed are soft of soul; this is referred to the female. Those whose back between the shoulders is excessively humped, with the shoulders drawn in toward the chest, are of bad character; this is referred to appropriateness, because what ought to appear in front is hidden from view.

Those who have the back between the shoulders hollowed backward are frivolous and foolish; this is referred to horses. But since it ought to be neither too humped nor too hollow, the mean of what is well-formed must be sought.

Those whose shoulder-tops and shoulders are well-jointed are stout of soul; this is referred to the male. Those whose shoulders are weak and ill-jointed are soft of soul; this is referred to the female — I say the same as was said of the feet and thighs.

Those whose shoulders move freely are free in soul; this is referred by way of appearance, because liberality is fitting to a form that appears thus. Those whose shoulders move with difficulty, drawn together, are illiberal; this is referred to appropriateness.

Those whose collarbones move freely are perceptive; for, the region of the collarbones being free-moving, they easily receive the motions of the senses. Those whose collarbones are pressed close together are dull of sense; for, that region being immovable, they are unable to receive the motion of the senses. Those who have a thick neck are stout of soul;

this is referred to the male. Those who have a thin neck are weak; this is referred to the female. Those with a thick, full neck are spirited; this is referred to spirited bulls. Those with a neck of good size, not overly thick, are magnanimous; this is referred to lions. Those with a thin, long neck are cowardly; this is referred to deer. Those with an excessively short neck are treacherous; this is referred to wolves.

Those whose lips are thin, and slack at their outer edges, such that the part of the upper lip near the corners overlaps the lower, are magnanimous; this is referred to lions. One might observe this too in large, vigorous dogs.

Those whose lips are thin and hard, with the region near the canine teeth raised, are, when so formed, well-bred; this is referred to swine. Those who have thick lips, with the upper hanging over the lower, are foolish; this is referred to asses and monkeys. Those who have the upper lip and gums protruding are fond of abuse; this is referred to dogs.

Those who have the tip of the nose thick are indolent; this is referred to oxen. Those who have the tip of the nose thick at the very point are dull of sense; this is referred to swine. Those who have the tip of the nose sharp are quick to anger; this is referred to dogs. Those who have the tip of the nose rounded but blunt are magnanimous; this is referred to lions.

Those who have the tip of the nose thin are bird-like. Those with a hooked nose, curving at once from the forehead, are shameless; this is referred to ravens. Those with a nose that is hooked but well-articulated from the forehead are magnanimous; this is referred to eagles.

Those who have a hollow nose, rounded in front of the forehead, the roundness rising upward, are lustful; this is referred to cocks. Those with a snub nose are lustful; this is referred to deer. Those whose nostrils are flared open are spirited; this is referred to the affection that occurs in spiritedness.

Those who have a fleshy face are indolent; this is referred to oxen. Those with a lean face are careful; those with a fleshy face are cowardly; this is referred to asses and deer. Those with a small face are mean-spirited; this is referred to cats and monkeys. Those with a large face are sluggish; this is referred to asses and oxen.
But since it ought to be neither small nor large, the mean state between these would be the fitting one. Those whose face appears mean and paltry are illiberal; this is referred to appropriateness.

Those who have, as it were, little pouches hanging beneath the eyes are wine-bibbers; this is referred to the affection, for those greatly given to drink have, before their eyes, something like little pouches standing out. Those who have this fond of sleep; this is referred to the affection, because those who have just risen from sleep have this hanging appearance about the eyes.

Those who have small eyes are mean-spirited; this is referred to appropriateness and to the monkey. Those who are large-eyed are sluggish; this is referred to oxen. The well-formed man, then, ought to have eyes neither small nor large. Those who have hollow eyes are mischievous; this is referred to the monkey. Those who are prominent-eyed are foolish; this is referred to appropriateness and to asses.

But since the eye ought to be neither prominent nor hollow, the mean condition would prevail. Those whose eyes are somewhat hollow are magnanimous; this is referred to lions. Those whose eyes are hollow to a greater degree are gentle; this is referred to oxen.

Those who have a small forehead are ignorant; this is referred to swine. Those with an excessively large forehead are sluggish; this is referred to oxen. Those with a rounded forehead are dull of sense; this is referred to asses. Those with a forehead longer and flat are dull of sense; this is referred to dogs.

Those who have a forehead square and well-proportioned are magnanimous; this is referred to lions. Those who have a clouded, lowering forehead are self-willed; this is referred to the bull and the lion. Those who have a serene, untroubled forehead are flatterers; this is referred to the affection that occurs — one might observe it in dogs, that when they fawn, they have a smooth, calm forehead.

Since, then, the clouded condition displays self-will and the serene displays flattery, the mean condition between the two would be the most fitting. Those with gloomy foreheads are prone to distress; this is referred to the affection, since those who are distressed are gloomy of countenance. Those who look downcast are mourners; this is referred to the affection, because those who mourn are downcast.

Those who have a large head are perceptive; this is referred to dogs. Those with a small head are dull of sense; this is referred to asses. Those with a pointed head are shameless; this is referred to the hook-taloned birds. Those with small ears are ape-like, and those with large ears ass-like; one might observe that the best of dogs, too, have ears of moderate size.

Those excessively black-skinned are cowardly; this is referred to Egyptians and Ethiopians. Those excessively white are also cowardly; this is referred to women. The colour that contributes to courage must be a mean between these. The tawny-haired are stout of soul; this is referred to lions. Those of excessively reddish colour are utter rogues; this is referred to foxes.

Those pallid and troubled in colour are cowardly; this is referred to the affection that arises from fear. Those of honey-pale colour are chilled; and things chilled are hard to move; and, their bodies being hard to move, they would be sluggish. Those whose colour is red are quick, because everything in the body that grows hot from motion turns red.

Those whose colour is flame-like are prone to madness, because things in the body, when excessively heated, take on a flame-like hue; and those extremely heated would be prone to madness. Those whose colour about the chest is inflamed are quick to anger; this is referred to the affection, for in those who grow angry the region about the chest becomes inflamed.

Those in whom the veins about the neck and temples are stretched taut are quick to anger; this is referred to the affection, because this happens to those who are angry. Those whose face turns crimson are easily shamed; this is referred to the affection, because the face of those who feel shame turns crimson.

Those whose cheeks turn crimson are wine-bibbers; this is referred to the affection, because the cheeks of those who are drunk turn crimson. Those whose eyes turn crimson are prone to fits of rage; this is referred to the affection, because those who are beside themselves with anger have their eyes turn crimson.

Those whose eyes are excessively black are cowardly, for an excessively black colour has appeared to signify cowardice. Those not excessively black, but inclining toward tawny, are stout of soul. Those whose eyes are pale grey or white are cowardly; for a white colour has appeared to signify cowardice. Those not pale grey but of a bright grey-blue are stout of soul; this is referred to the lion and the eagle.

Those whose eyes are wine-dark are wanton; this is referred to goats. Those whose eyes are fiery are shameless; this is referred to dogs. Those pale-eyed, with troubled eyes, are cowardly; this is referred to the affection, because those who have been frightened turn pale, their colour uneven. Those whose eyes are glistening are lustful; this is referred to cocks and ravens.

Those with shaggy shins are lustful; this is referred to goats. Those excessively shaggy about the chest and belly never remain steadfast in the same pursuits; this is referred to birds, because these have the chest and belly shaggiest of all. Those with an excessively bare chest are shameless; this is referred to women. Since, then, it ought to be neither excessively shaggy nor bare, the mean condition is the best.

Those with shaggy shoulders never remain constant in the same pursuits; this is referred to birds. Those with an excessively shaggy back are shameless; this is referred to beasts. Those with a shaggy neck at the back are free-spirited; this is referred to lions. Those bearded only at the chin's edge are stout of soul; this is referred to dogs.

Those with joined eyebrows are prone to distress; this is referred to the resemblance of the affection. Those whose eyebrows are drawn down toward the nose and raised toward the temple are simple-minded; this is referred to swine. Those with bristling hair upon the head are cowardly; this is referred to the affection, because those who become frightened also bristle.

Those with excessively curly hair are cowardly; this is referred to Ethiopians. Since, then, both bristling hair and excessively curly hair indicate cowardice, hair with a slight curl would tend toward stoutness of soul; this too is referred to the lion.

Those whose forehead-hair inclines back toward the crown of the head are free-spirited; this is referred to lions. Those whose hair grows down upon the forehead toward the nose are illiberal; this is referred to appropriateness, because the appearance is slavish.

The long-strider and the slow-strider would be sluggish, given to excess, deliberate, because striding far is effective, while striding slowly is procrastinating. The short-strider and slow-strider is sluggish, given to excess, and not effective, because striding short and slowly is not effective. The long-strider and quick-strider is not given to excess, but effective, because quickness is effective, while length is not.

The short-strider and quick-strider is given to excess, but not effective. Concerning the carriage of the hand, forearm, and upper arm, the same signs apply. Those who sway at the shoulders, holding them upright and outstretched, are crook-armed; this is referred to horses.

Those who sway at the shoulders, stooping forward, are magnanimous; this is referred to lions. Those who walk with their feet turned outward, and with feminine shins, are referred to women. Those who bend and rub their bodies together as they move are flatterers; this is referred to the affection.

Those who lean to the right as they walk are effeminate; this is referred to appropriateness. Those with quick-moving eyes, keen-sighted, are rapacious; this is referred to hawks. Those who blink are cowardly, because in their eyes they are the first to turn away.

Those with a kind of downward droop, and those in whom one eyelid overlaps the eyes, standing in the middle of the field of vision, and those who draw their gaze up beneath the upper lids, looking softly, and those with drooping eyelids, and, in general, all those who look with a soft and languid gaze, are referred to appropriateness and to women.

Those who move their eyes but slowly over a long time, and have a whitish tinge upon the eye, as though fixed in place, are contemplative; for whenever the soul becomes intensely occupied with some thought, the gaze too comes to a stop.

Those who speak loudly in a deep tone are insolent; this is referred to asses. Those who speak beginning from a deep tone but ending in a shrill one are despondent, given to lamenting; this is referred to oxen, and to what is fitting to the voice. Those who converse in high-pitched, soft, broken tones are effeminate; this is referred to women and to appropriateness.

Those who speak in a loud, deep, unbroken tone are referred to vigorous dogs and to appropriateness. Those who speak in a soft, toneless voice are gentle; this is referred to sheep. Those who speak in a shrill, screeching voice are wanton; this is referred to goats.

Those excessively small are keen, because the movement of the blood, occupying a small space, arrives very quickly at the seat of understanding. Those excessively large are slow, because the movement of the blood, occupying a large space, arrives slowly at the seat of understanding.

As many of the small as use dry flesh, or such colours as arise upon the body through heat, accomplish nothing; for the movement of the blood, being confined in a small space and swift on account of its fiery quality, never remains fixed upon the same thought, but shifts from one thing to another before it has brought the matter at hand to completion.

As many of the large as use excessively moist flesh, or such colours as arise through cold, likewise accomplish nothing; for the movement, occupying a large space and being slow on account of the coldness, does not succeed in arriving at the seat of understanding.

As many of the small as use moist flesh and colours arising through cold become effective; for the movement, occupying a small space, and the sluggishness of the temperament providing a due proportion, brings the matter first undertaken to completion.

As many of the large as use dry flesh and colours arising through heat become both effective and perceptive; for heat corrects the excess of size in the flesh and the colour, so that it becomes proportionate for bringing matters to completion.

It has now been stated how bodies that are excessive in size, or deficient in smallness, are, as it happens, both effective and, as it were, incomplete. The nature that is a mean between these is strongest for the senses and most effective in whatever it undertakes; for its motions, not having far to travel, arrive easily at the understanding, and, being neither excessive, do not overshoot it either.

So that the most perfect man, for bringing to completion whatever he sets before himself, and for perceiving what he is about to perceive, must be of moderate size. Those of disproportionate build are rogues; this is referred to the affection and to the female. For if the disproportionate are rogues, the proportionate would be just and courageous.

The reference of proportion, however, should be made to the tractability and good natural disposition of bodies, and not to the form proper to the male, as was distinguished at the outset. It is well, too, to refer all the signs already stated to appropriateness in both the male and the female; for these have received the most complete division of all, and it has been shown that the male is more just and more courageous than the female, and, to put it simply, better.

In the whole selection of signs, some signs indicate the underlying character more clearly than others. Clearer are those that occur in the most important regions of the body. The most important region is that about the eyes, the forehead, the head, and the face; the second is that about the chest and shoulders; then that about the legs and feet; the region about the belly is least important of all. In general, these regions furnish the clearest signs, since it is upon them, too, that the greatest degree of intelligent expression appears.
